System design · v1 · spec

Flow — Agentic Company OS

Goals become projects. Projects become cards. Cards become merged code. Code moves the metrics. Metrics reshape the goals. Flow is an operating loop where a fleet of AI agents does the running — planning, building, verifying, shipping, monitoring — and humans set direction, review where they choose to, or simply observe.

The goal

Run your team or startup in full autonomy:

  1. Install Flow. It integrates with the Kanban board you already have, or builds you one.
  2. Wire up the dashboard so every number lands in one place — engineering, KPIs, traffic, logs, spend.
  3. Give the agents a mission. They decompose it into projects, epics and tasks on the board.
  4. Let the orchestrator run them — epochs of agents working that board until the metric moves.

All of it on your AI subscriptions rather than metered API credits — with an exception for models cheap enough to justify on their own (Gemma 4, DeepSeek, Kimi 3, GLM 5.2) on summarization and other non-mission-critical work.

Human Agent System Data / metrics

Three layers, and Chat — Slack and e-mail, where every human/agent touchpoint happens — sitting above them. Humans set direction into the Plan Layer: mission, quarterly goals and KPIs, the persistent projects under them, and the board those projects decompose into. An agent can also be addressed directly, straight into the Execution Layer, where interchangeable harnesses — Claude Code and Codex on subscription, AI agents on API inference — open PRs that run through verify, merge and deploy into releases. The Monitor Layer is where every number lands: monitoring agents read the dashboard, file new work onto the board, and send insights back to the plan — the return stops there, never at the mission. Underneath it all, the knowledge every agent reads on boot and writes back to after each run.

01Mission

The highest-level object. Only a human may change it.

The mission defines what the company exists to accomplish, and it is the long-term constraint under which every goal, project and agent operates. Unlike everything downstream, it can only be created or changed by the human operator. Agents may read it, plan against it, ask clarifying questions and flag conflicts — but they cannot rewrite it, and no metric, anomaly or evaluation is allowed to.

A mission should stay stable for roughly a year. It is not measured directly: humans translate it into the quarterly goals and KPIs the system can actually act on, and every goal, project, epic and task must be traceable back to it.

Missions look like this
  • Ensure everyone can own and benefit from AI.
  • Make professional software development accessible to any small team.
  • Build the most trusted technical community for frontier AI.

This replaces the assumption that a planning agent creates a new project every week. A weekly ritual may still create or prioritise work, but a project is a persistent strategic container holding successive epics — not a disposable weekly plan.

02Goals, KPIs & planning horizons

The mission, translated into numbers the system can act on.

Humans define the company's goals and KPIs, normally once per quarter. Each goal connects a strategic outcome to one or more measurable indicators — "grow newsletter signups 25%", "p75 LCP under 2s". Agents can recommend goals, surface metric gaps and propose changes, but the final goals and targets stay human-controlled. Each goal also carries guardrail metrics, so the system cannot improve one number by quietly damaging another: a signup-growth goal watches unsubscribe rate, spam complaints, signup quality, acquisition cost and page performance alongside the number it is trying to move.

Below the goals, work is decomposed by agents and the horizons get shorter at every level:

  • Mission — approximately one year.
  • Goals and KPIs — approximately one quarter.
  • Projects and features — open for as long as they remain a valid way of reaching a goal.
  • Epics — bounded bodies of work inside a project.
  • Tasks and bugs — short execution units an agent can claim and finish.
Projects are containers, not weekly plans A planning agent does not create a new project every week. A weekly ritual may still create or reprioritise work, but a project is a persistent strategic container that can hold many successive epics and outlive several goal cycles. As metrics change, agents create new epics, revise planned ones, or recommend closing the project outright.

That traceability is what lets the evaluator ask, months after a change shipped, whether it actually moved the number it was created to move.

03Kanban board

The single interface between humans and agents.

All work is a card. The hierarchy runs mission → goal → project → epic → task/bug; cards cross-link with dependencies, and every card carries its own execution policy — which model runs it, at what effort, and how much autonomy it gets. Mission and goals are visible on a card as linked strategic context, but they do not travel through the execution columns — only epics, tasks and bugs do. Humans and agents use the same board: drag a card, and an agent picks it up; an agent finishes, and the card moves under your cursor. A card that can't proceed right now — blocked on an answer, an external event, or something to revisit later — parks in To follow up instead of clogging the active lanes, then rejoins the flow when it's unblocked.

04Workflow Graph / Agent Orchestrator

A third board view that is the execution plan.

Board and List answer what is on the plate. Workflow Graph answers in what order it can run — and it is the same structure the orchestrator executes, not a drawing of it. Every epic renders as its own self-contained DAG (nodes are tasks, edges are dependencies) laid out against a shared ready-epoch axis, so horizontal position is execution order rather than layout aesthetics. Task edges never leave their epic: an epic graph is complete on its own, which is exactly what lets the orchestrator dispatch one epoch of one epic without reasoning about the rest of the board. The only place two epics touch is the project layer, drawn here as the left-hand rail — a project-level edge from epic A to epic B is a gate, and when it opens, B's whole graph becomes ready and therefore starts further right on the epoch axis.

Node fill is card state — grey done, green an agent is running it, amber waiting on a dependency. Epic A occupies epochs 1–3; epic B is gated by A at the project layer, so its own epoch 1 lands on the board's epoch 4; epic C shares no edge with either and starts immediately.

  • The ready set is a column. Everything in the leftmost unfinished epoch of an epic is dispatchable right now — that is the orchestrator's next epoch, read straight off the chart instead of inferred from a plan.
  • Critical path is visible. The longest chain inside an epic graph is that epic's floor on wall-clock; adding agents widens the columns, it never shortens the chain.
  • "Why isn't this running?" is one hop. An amber node either waits on siblings you can see, or on the single project edge feeding its epic card.
  • Epics stay independently schedulable. Because no task edge crosses the boundary, an epic can be re-planned, paused, or re-run without recomputing any other epic's DAG.
Write-time validation A task dependency is accepted only when both cards resolve to the same parent_id epic; a link drawn between two epics is stored as a project-level gate on the epic cards, and a dep that would close a cycle is refused outright. Every rejection lands in the card log with its reason, so the graph is a DAG by construction rather than by nightly repair.

Executing it

An agent picks its own scope: a whole epic, or a few tasks inside one. Both are safe precisely because the epic graph is self-contained — taking the epic means owning its epochs end to end; taking a slice means claiming individual cards out of the current ready epoch and leaving the rest of the graph to whoever else shows up. The orchestrator walks each epic graph, takes the leftmost unfinished epoch, and dispatches one agent per card into its own git worktree. It is harness-agnostic: each card goes to whichever coding agent its policy names (Claude Code, Codex, or an API-driven worker). Approved-but-unmerged PRs are merged first on every cycle, so finished work never queues behind new work — and merging is what clears the deps that promote the next epoch.

Claiming a card

Before touching anything, an agent assigns the card to itself and then moves it to in progress. That column move is the signal — it is how every other agent (and every human watching the board) learns the card is taken. A card carries one worker in practice, but the assignment field holds two, so a race is recorded rather than lost. When two workers land on the same card, the one with the lowest claim timestamp decides: keep the card, or leave it to the other agent. The decision is explicit and logged; nobody silently steals work, and no card ends up with two agents editing it.

  • Assign, then move. Self-assignment and the move to in progress are one atomic step; an agent that can't do both doesn't start.
  • Two slots, one worker. The second slot exists to make contention visible — it is never a licence for two agents to work the same card.
  • Earliest claim arbitrates. Lowest timestamp holds the decision right, which makes the outcome deterministic and replayable from the log.
  • Stale claims expire. A worker that stops heartbeating loses its slot, and the card returns to the ready epoch rather than sitting occupied.

Agent signaling — TBD

The board covers status signals well: claim a card, move a column, comment on a card, and everyone converges on the next poll. What's still open is agent-to-agent signaling — pushing updates, changes, and notifications between running agents without round-tripping through the board: "I changed the shape of this module", "my card is going to break yours", "stop, I've already fixed that". Polling a card log is a poor substitute for a message bus.

Open question Design a signaling channel for live agents — delivery, ordering, and who is allowed to interrupt whom. Action: ask @dan van flyman about Synapse before we build anything here; it may already be the answer.
Note — we don't build the harness We're not trying to improve the harness — many teams are already working on that. Instead, our orchestrator delegates work to the existing harnesses, which serves two purposes:
  1. we use our subscription tokens, saving money;
  2. we take advantage of the existing harness — the system improves as the harness improves.

05Agents — engineers, operators, QA & judges

The workforce. One isolated workspace each.

Engineer agents build: each gets a fresh git worktree (a full checkout with dependencies linked in), so parallel agents never collide on files. The pipeline is fixed: branch → implement → lint → test → push → open PR → report back. Operator agents run the non-code work — content, emails, triage, scheduled rituals. QA & judge agents monitor the platform — sweeps, verification scoring, anomaly watching — and create new tickets, or alert the user when something's off. Every agent keeps durable state: a memory.md of what it has learned, and a per-run steps.md trail of what it did, so knowledge compounds across runs and any run is auditable.

Running on subscriptions, not credits

The economics are a design constraint, not an afterthought. Mission-critical work runs on the AI subscriptions you already pay for — the Claude Code and Codex seats sitting on your desk — so the bill stays flat as you add agents, and the system gets better every time those harnesses do. Metered API credits are the exception, reserved for models cheap enough to justify on their own merits: Gemma 4, DeepSeek, Kimi 3, GLM 5.2 and friends, on summarization, labelling, dedup and digest work where a wrong answer costs a retry rather than a bad merge. Every card's model + effort policy is what routes it, so the split is a per-card decision you can see and override.

The router is the same model/effort resolution the board already does per card — routing by cost class rather than by capability alone is the only addition.

06Verification loop

Quality as a number, enforced by a loop.

A card can declare a goal percentage. When it does, an independent verification agent scores the finished work 0–100 against the card's intent. Below the bar, the work goes back — same branch, same PR, with the score's critique attached — until it passes or the card's loop limit is spent. Every attempt is logged on the card, so the cost of quality is visible, not hidden.

Two levels of evaluation

Verification is not the only judgment the system makes. Task or PR verification runs before merge and asks whether the implementation satisfies the card. Epic result evaluation runs after all the work is complete — and, where the completion policy requires it, after deployment metrics have arrived — and asks whether the finished body of work achieved its intended result. A card can pass every gate in the first level and still belong to an epic that failed the second.

07Epic completion & result evaluation

Finishing the tasks is not the same as achieving the result.

Completing every task in an epic does not mean the epic succeeded. When the last task lands, an independent evaluation agent reviews the epic's original intent, the completed tasks and merged PRs, the verification scores and test results, the deployment status, the relevant product or business metrics, and any regressions or incidents that appeared along the way. It then records a completion assessment.

  • Completed successfully — the intended result was delivered.
  • Completed, awaiting metrics — the implementation is finished, but the outcome needs more data before it can be judged.
  • Partially completed — the work shipped, but the intended result was not fully achieved.
  • Needs improvement — the evaluator creates a follow-up epic.
  • Invalidated — the underlying assumption was wrong, and the project itself should be reconsidered.

When improvement is required the evaluator creates a new epic or proposes a change to the project. It does not silently reopen completed tasks — an epic that stays permanently open because optional improvements were discovered tells you nothing about whether the original intent was met.

Two separate controls Task verification asks whether the implementation satisfies the card, and it runs before merge. Epic evaluation asks whether the completed body of work achieved its intended result, and it runs after all the work is done and — where the card's completion policy requires it — after deployment metrics have arrived.

08Autonomy — automerge vs. review

Trust is a per-card dial, not a global switch.

Every card decides how much freedom its agent gets. Marked automerge, the agent squash-merges its own passing PR and the card lands in Done untouched by human hands. Otherwise the card parks in Review and waits for a verdict: approve, and an agent merges it; request changes, and the feedback goes back to the same agent on the same branch. Low-stakes work flows friction-free; high-stakes work keeps a human gate — on exactly the cards you choose.

09Run tracker

Every unit of agent work is a tracked, stateful run.

Runs form a tree in Postgres — orchestrator → epoch → task — and each run moves through an explicit state machine with a heartbeat. A run that stops beating goes stale and can be revived or reaped; a run that hits a question a human must answer pauses in needs-feedback rather than guessing. Nothing an agent does is invisible: every state, timestamp, prompt, and outcome is queryable.

10Agents Manager UI

Watch the fleet work, live.

A real-time view of the run tree: which orchestrator is active, which epochs are open, what every task agent is doing right now, and where a run is waiting on you. This is where a human answers a paused run's question, inspects a live console, or kills something — fleet observability in one screen.

The needs-feedback chip is the human inbox: click it, answer the agent's question, and the run resumes.

11Two CLIs

Headless hands for agents working in isolated worktrees.

Worktrees don't carry the app's runtime, so all reads and writes go through two small command-line tools. todo-cli is the board: read the plan, update a card, attach a PR, leave a comment. agent-cli is the run lifecycle: start a run, heartbeat, ask a human, finish — plus durable memory reads and writes. Everything an agent does to shared state flows through these two audited doors.

12Self-feeding sweeps

The system finds its own bugs while everyone sleeps.

Nightly, a visual-QA sweep screenshots every route on desktop and mobile and has a vision model judge them; a performance sweep scores the same routes on speed and web vitals. Findings become bug cards — deduplicated by title, so a known issue never files twice — dropped straight into Todo at a priority matching their severity. By morning, the board has already triaged the night's regressions.

13Runner daemon

The always-on autopilot.

A long-running process that makes the loop continuous instead of on-demand. It scans the board, claims ready cards race-safely (two daemons never grab the same card), executes each through the standard worktree pipeline, merges or parks the result per the card's autonomy policy, and alerts a human — Telegram, SMS — only when something genuinely needs one. With the daemon on, filing a card is shipping the feature.

14Dashboard

A core component, not a reporting page attached to one.

The dashboard is the single surface where every measurable thing the company produces lands: business results, product usage, engineering health, delivery throughput, cost, and agent performance. Humans read it to decide direction. Agents read it to decide work. Because both audiences share one set of numbers, a goal, the work created to move it, and the evidence that it moved are never held in separate systems.

It is an API as much as a page — the data behind every view is queryable, and most of its readers are not human:

  • Planning agents read KPI gaps, guardrails and historical project impact when proposing projects and epics.
  • The evaluation agent reads outcome metrics when deciding whether a completed epic achieved its intended result.
  • Scheduled jobs and standing agents read thresholds and trends to detect anomalies and file work.
  • The execution-policy router reads agent performance to decide which configuration receives the next card.

The major views are Strategy (mission, quarterly goals and KPIs, projects, epics and the strategic Gantt), Agent performance (the quarterly agent OKRs), plus business and product, engineering and delivery, and anomalies.

One surface, five views, two audiences. Humans read it to decide direction; the planning, evaluation, monitoring and routing agents read the same numbers through the API to decide work. Instrumentation is itself a tracked metric — an outcome nobody measured cannot be evaluated.

Two properties make it trustworthy enough for agents to act on unattended. First, instrumentation is part of the work: a card expected to move a measurable outcome is not complete until the metric that would prove it exists and reports, and missing instrumentation is itself a ticket. Second, attribution is explicit — metric movement is labelled direct, modeled or correlated rather than collapsed into a single causal number. Goals sit beside the metrics that measure them, so "are we winning" and "is the machine healthy" become the same glance.

15Strategic Gantt view

The long-range view of the company, over time.

The Workflow Graph answers what can run next. The Gantt answers where the company is against its year. It covers mission, quarterly goals and KPIs, projects and epics — tasks stay in the Kanban and Workflow Graph views, where they belong, and generally do not appear here at all.

  • Planned and actual dates — start and end, side by side, so slippage is visible rather than inferred.
  • Status and percent complete — on track, at risk, blocked, or complete.
  • Relationships — which projects serve which goal, and which epics sit inside which project.
  • Project-level gates — the epic-to-epic dependencies that decide when a gated epic can start.
  • The metric trend for each goal, beside the bar that claims to move it.
  • Projects that span more than one cycle, drawn crossing the boundary rather than truncated at it.
  • Epics awaiting outcome data — deployed, but not yet judged.

Mission, goals, projects, epics — tasks stay in the Kanban and Workflow Graph views. Percent complete blends task completion, epic evaluation scores, deployment status and observed KPI impact; the Workflow Graph remains the authority on what can actually run.

Percent complete is not card count A project can read as 90% done while having moved nothing. Progress at every level blends task completion with the epic evaluation score, the deployment status and the observed KPI impact — which is why an epic can sit at deployed, awaiting metrics instead of jumping straight to complete.

16Monitoring & improvement agents

The part of the company that never stops paying attention.

Standing watchers evaluate trigger conditions against the metric stream — error spikes, metric anomalies, degrading trends. When one fires, an investigate agent digs in: reads logs, reproduces, identifies the likely cause, and files a card with its findings attached. A slower-cadence insights agent reads analytics for opportunities rather than fires — and files improvement cards the same way. This is what closes the loop: the system doesn't just execute the backlog, it writes it.

17Agent OKRs & performance

Scorecards for the fleet — not company goals for agents.

Agent OKRs are quarterly scorecards used to understand which models, harnesses, agent configurations and execution policies actually perform. Their purpose is routing and accountability across the fleet; they do not give agents independent objectives of their own. An agent identity is the whole configuration — model, version, harness, system prompt, skills, tool permissions, effort level and memory setup — because that is the unit whose performance you can actually act on.

  • Throughput — cards completed, epics contributed to, cycle time.
  • Quality — first-attempt success rate, verification scores, number of rework loops, PR approval versus rejection.
  • Consequences — regressions or incidents introduced, merge reverts, test, lint and build outcomes, code-quality signals where measurable.
  • Cost — token usage and cost per accepted card.
  • Independence — how many human interventions the work required.

KPI impact needs care. A card or epic may contribute to a metric change without being its sole cause, so Flow distinguishes direct attribution, modeled attribution and simple correlation rather than presenting all metric movement as agent-created. Performance then feeds back into the execution-policy router: over time the system learns which configuration is most reliable for migrations, frontend work, debugging, planning, review and content — and routes accordingly. Promotion and demotion are policy, and both are recorded and reversible.

18Agent knowledge, memory & self-improvement

What the system learns, it keeps — and uses.

Every agent boots with the system prompt — the constitution: who the company is, what it values, the rules that never change. Beyond that, knowledge lives in five stores:

  • agent.md — per-agent memory. Durable lessons an agent carries between runs — conventions, gotchas, preferences it has learned — plus the steps.md trail of what it did and why.
  • skills.md — shared playbooks. Step-by-step procedures for recurring work (deploys, migrations, review checklists) written once and loadable by any agent on demand; when an agent figures out a better way, the skill is updated for everyone.
  • Code knowledge — the code hierarchy, cached. A script extracts the current hierarchy of the codebase — what lives where, how it connects — and re-runs each time a PR is created, so it never goes stale. Agents read it on boot for a warm start instead of rediscovering the repo cold every run.
  • Company knowledge (RAG) — everything the business knows: docs, decisions, product specs, emails, brand voice. The admin decides what is stored here and how — a Karpathy-style Obsidian second brain, a typical RAG pipeline, or a set of tools that connects the company's services — and any agent retrieves from it at the moment it's needed, so a week-one agent works with years of context.
  • Memory — experimental. After each run the agent distills something worth remembering, and that memory is shared across coding agents — Codex, Claude Code, Open Code, plain API — so a lesson learned on one harness is available to all of them.

Self-improvement is the loop across all five: every run ends by distilling its outcome into the right store, so the next run starts smarter. And because every run is a snapshot (the exact prompt plus the repo commit it ran against), any card can be rolled back and forked: multiple attempts branch from the same snapshot, verification scores pick the winner, and the run tree becomes a search over approaches. The company doesn't just do the work — it gets better at doing the work.

Top: the learning loop — outcomes are distilled into memory that the next run reads. Bottom: because runs are snapshots, attempts fork and the verification score (or the user) picks which branch continues.

19Installation

One line, pasted into Claude Code. The agent does the rest.

Flow installs by instruction, not by package manager. There is nothing to download and no dependency to add. You paste a single line into a coding agent already running in your project, and that agent performs the installation itself — reading the repository, creating the skill, mounting the board, building the dashboard, and proving it works before it stops:

claude "Install Flow in this project: read github.com/AISocratic/flow, then follow install.md top to bottom."

The same line works with any other coding agent:

codex "Install Flow in this project: read github.com/AISocratic/flow, then follow install.md top to bottom."

How it works

There is no Flow package to add and no Flow runtime to run. The repository carries an install.md written for the agent rather than for a human, and the agent executes it as a sequence of checked steps:

  • Read the repository. The agent fetches the repo, reads install.md, and reads the spec it references before changing anything.
  • Check preconditions. A git repo, a clean working tree, and — if you are integrating rather than running standalone — an existing authenticated admin area.
  • Cut a snapshot branch. flow/pre-install is created before the first edit, so a complete revert always exists.
  • Detect the stack. It reads package.json, pyproject.toml, Cargo.toml or go.mod and records the test, lint and build commands you already have. It records your commands; it does not add its own.
  • Install the skill. flow-agent-orchestrator is the only mandatory change to your repo — it is what teaches any agent to read the board, plan epochs, dispatch work and merge.
  • Mount the board and orchestrator, integrated behind your auth or as a standalone panel.
  • Create the dashboard. Metric tables, views and collectors are wired to whatever the project already emits, so the strategy and agent-performance views have data from the first cycle.
  • Configure execution policy — default model, effort, autonomy, verification thresholds and merge policy, all overridable per card.
  • Run a smoke test. Installation is not finished until one real card has travelled from Todo to an open PR under your own CI.
  • Report what it created, what it skipped, and how to remove it.

If a step cannot be satisfied, the agent stops and reports rather than improvising around it.

What it drops into

The goal is that Flow drops into any project and runs on the toolchain that is already installed — JS, Python, Rust, Go, whatever the repo speaks. It adds no runtime dependency and no build step of its own: it discovers your test, lint, and build commands and calls them. An agent already running on your machine should know what to do after one addition to the repo — the flow-agent-orchestrator skill. Nothing else.

Where the orchestrator lives is a separate choice. It can run as a standalone admin panel beside your platform, or be integrated into it. Integrated is the better solution: it inherits your RBAC/ACL — the same users, roles, and permissions — sits on the same database, and shares the general knowledge your platform already encodes, so agents read your domain instead of guessing at it.

The install is one skill plus an agent-executed install.md; the deployment shape is the only real decision. Uninstalling removes the orchestrator, not the work it did — that lives in git like any other commit.

Uninstall

Removal is easy: delete the skill, drop the board routes, drop (or keep) the orchestrator tables. What removal does not undo is the work the agents did — those are ordinary commits in your repo, and the only way to fully revert them is git checkout flow/pre-install.

Test it thoroughly — and be ready to revert Run it on a real but non-critical part of the backlog first, with automerge off, and read the PRs. Keep the snapshot branch until you're satisfied, and revert everything if it isn't working for you. We strongly believe that once you've tried the orchestrator, you won't roll back.

20Problems & Solutions

Known failure modes — and the design's answer to each.

  • Hallucinations & agent drift — small hallucinations are expected and compound over time, and agents drift the longer they run. The answer is twofold: scout agents run regularly overnight, fixing bugs and re-verifying the code before drift becomes debt; and the user periodically makes sure the projects are in a good state, so drift gets corrected before it spreads.
  • Platform errors — bugs and errors are caught live by the monitors and solved via self-healing: the monitor files the ticket, an agent fixes it on the next cycle. Any mission-critical task is reviewed and approved by the user before it deploys — or at minimum reviewed by an agent judge.

The flywheel

Each pass around the loop compounds. Shipped work moves the metrics; metrics expose the next gap; monitoring turns the gap into cards; agents turn cards into shipped work — and the agents' memories mean every pass is a little sharper than the last. The system's output is not just features: it is an ever-better version of itself.

Humans set direction

Define goals, adjust targets, decide what the company is for. Everything downstream is derived.

Humans gate what they choose

Per-card autonomy means review effort concentrates exactly where judgment matters — and nowhere else.

Humans can just watch

Manager UI and dashboards make the whole machine legible in real time. Observing is a valid mode of operation.
